tagline: Poland's former textile powerhouse turns red-brick factories into museums, lofts and shopping streets, with long Piotrkowska Street, murals and a famous film school.
overview: Łódź grew from a small town into Poland's industrial giant in the 19th century, when textile mills drew workers and entrepreneurs from across Europe. Polish, Jewish, German and Russian communities built the city together, and its palaces of factory owners still stand beside rows of red-brick mills.

Piotrkowska Street, about 4 km long, is the city's main promenade, lined with restored townhouses, restaurants and bars. Manufaktura, the former Poznański textile works, is now a huge complex of shops, a hotel and the Museum of the Factory, while the OFF Piotrkowska courtyard is full of bars and creative studios.

The National Film School in Łódź trained Roman Polański, Andrzej Wajda and Krzysztof Kieślowski, earning the city the nickname 'Hollywoodż'. Large murals cover many walls, and the Jewish Cemetery and Radegast Station recall the wartime ghetto.
